content: The Firmicutes are a group of bacteria that predominantly exhibit a Gram-positive cell wall structure. However, some members of this group, such as the Mollicutes (commonly referred to as mycoplasmas), lack a cell wall entirely. As a result, these bacteria do not respond to Gram staining. Despite this, they also lack the second outer membrane that is characteristic of Gram-negative bacteria. Additionally, certain Firmicutes, such as Megasphaera, Pectinatus, Selenomonas, and Zymophilus, possess a porous pseudo-outer membrane, which causes them to stain Gram-negative despite their classification. Historically, the Firmicutes were thought to encompass all Gram-positive bacteria. However, more recent classifications have narrowed this group to a core set of related bacteria, often referred to as the low G+C group, in contrast to the Actinobacteria, which are characterized by a higher G+C content in their DNA. Morphologically, Firmicutes can appear as spherical cells (cocci) or rod-shaped forms. Many members of this phylum are capable of producing endospores, which are highly resistant to desiccation and can survive in extreme environmental conditions. Firmicutes are found in a wide range of environments and include several notable pathogenic species. One family within this phylum, the heliobacteria, is unique in that its members are capable of photosynthesis to generate energy. Additionally, Firmicutes play a significant role in the spoilage of beer, wine, and cider. However, due to the high phenotypic diversity within this phylum, which is partly attributed to the frequent exchange of plasmids across species and genera, there is currently no definitive method to identify a bacterium as belonging to the Firmicutes phylum based solely on its characteristics. In the context of human health, Firmicutes are an important component of the gut microbiota. Research has demonstrated their involvement in energy absorption and their potential role in the development of obesity. Classes of Firmicutes The Firmicutes phylum is typically divided into three main classes: Clostridia, Bacilli, and Mollicutes. Clostridia: These bacteria are anaerobic, meaning they thrive in environments devoid of oxygen. Bacilli: Members of this class can be either obligate aerobes (requiring oxygen) or facultative aerobes (capable of surviving with or without oxygen). Mollicutes: This class includes bacteria that lack a cell wall entirely. Phylogenetic analyses have shown that the Clostridia and Bacilli classes, as well as their primary genera (Clostridium and Bacillus), are paraphyletic or polyphyletic. This suggests that these groups may undergo taxonomic revisions in the future. Genera within Firmicutes The Firmicutes phylum currently includes over 274 recognized genera. Some of the most notable genera are as follows: Bacilli (Order: Bacillales) Bacillus: Includes species known for their ability to form endospores and their use in industrial and medical applications. Listeria: Contains pathogenic species such as Listeria monocytogenes, which can cause listeriosis. Staphylococcus: Includes species like Staphylococcus aureus, a common cause of skin infections and other diseases. Bacilli (Order: Lactobacillales) Enterococcus: Includes species that are part of the normal gut flora but can also cause opportunistic infections. Lactobacillus: Known for their role in fermentation and as probiotics. Lactococcus: Commonly used in the production of dairy products like cheese. Leuconostoc: Involved in fermentation processes, particularly in food production. Pectinatus: Associated with beer spoilage. Pediococcus: Used in food fermentation but can also spoil alcoholic beverages. Streptococcus: Includes both commensal and pathogenic species, such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Streptococcus pyogenes. Clostridia Acetobacterium: Known for their role in anaerobic fermentation. Clostridium: Includes species such as Clostridium botulinum and Clostridium difficile, which are associated with severe diseases. Eubacterium: Part of the normal gut microbiota. Heliobacterium: Photosynthetic bacteria found in soil and water. Heliospirillum: A less well-known genus. Sporomusa: Involved in anaerobic metabolic processes. Mollicutes Mycoplasma: Includes species that are pathogenic to humans, such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Spiroplasma: Known for their association with plants and insects. Ureaplasma: Includes species that can cause infections in the urogenital tract. Erysipelothrix: Includes Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, which can cause erysipelas in animals and humans.
